analysis.one_liner: Gives every adult voter $100 vouchers per federal election to fund candidates of their choice.
analysis.headline: The bill was never considered: it sat in the Senate Rules Committee with no cosponsors and no vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a 'Democracy Dollars' program: any adult citizen could request $100 in vouchers for each federal primary and general election and give them to participating candidates, who would be paid from the Treasury. In exchange, participating candidates would have to accept only small individual contributions (starting at $1,000 per person and stepping down to $200 by 2029) and spend no more than $2,500 of their own money. The bill also repealed the old presidential public financing system and replaced it with this voucher program.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters would gain a way to fund candidates without spending their own money, and candidates who cannot tap wealthy donors or their own fortunes would gain a funding base. Participating candidates would get public money for every voucher they attract, and communities that historically give little to campaigns would be targeted for outreach.

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible adult could request $100 in vouchers per office per election cycle — congressional, Senate, and presidential — and direct them to participating candidates [S3].
Participating candidates could only accept individual contributions of $1,000 per person in 2021, stepping down to $200 per person by 2029, shrinking the power of big individual checks [S3].
Candidates could spend no more than $2,500 of their own (or immediate family) money per election, lowering the barrier for candidates who are not wealthy [S3].
The FEC would run outreach aimed at people who have not previously contributed to campaigns, and a pilot program would mail vouchers to broaden participation [S3].
Voucher recipients' identities would be largely shielded from public disclosure to protect their privacy [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the vouchers through an open-ended appropriation — 'such sums as necessary' with no dollar cap — plus the cost of administration, audits, and outreach. Non-participating candidates and the existing system of large contributions would also face candidates who no longer depend on wealthy donors.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as necessary' with no dollar limit, so the cost depends entirely on how many voters request vouchers, and amounts would grow if non-participating candidates' fundraising outpaced the program [S3].

Participation is voluntary: a candidate could skip the program, raise unlimited large-donor money at current limits, and outspend a participating rival, which is why the bill builds in automatic voucher increases if non-participating candidates outraise participants [S3].

The bill repeals the existing presidential public financing system (the $3 tax-checkoff fund) and moves leftover funds to the general Treasury, replacing one program rather than adding to it [S2][S3].
Voters would bear no out-of-pocket cost, but public money would flow to candidates across the political spectrum, including candidates a given taxpayer disagrees with.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the dominance of large donors directly: it hands every voter a meaningful amount of campaign money while cutting the amount any single donor can give. The honest costs are that the total price tag is uncapped by design, the program is voluntary so well-funded candidates could stay outside it, and administering a nationwide voucher system would be a significant new job for the FEC. Whether the public funding buys enough candidate competition to be worth the taxpayer cost is the genuine trade-off the bill asks Congress to judge.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the bill on May 1, 2019; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration [S1][S5].
No committee hearing, markup, or floor action followed, and the bill attracted no cosponsors [S4][S5].
The bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent lawmakers and the current campaign financing system are better off: large individual contributions stayed at their existing limits, and no public voucher program was created. The loss for voters is not a new burden but a forgone alternative to big-donor financing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big donors and the campaign status quo

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Elections Act and the Democracy Dollars public voucher program.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Roy Blunt
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never advanced the bill to a hearing or vote.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Senate leadership historically opposed public financing of campaigns and brought no such bill to the floor during the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so there is no roll call; the visible support was one Senate Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party, and the committee that buried it was controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: Participating candidates could accept only $1,000 per individual donor in 2021, falling to $200 by 2029, sharply cutting the value of a big check [S3]. Bundlers and major donors would lose influence over candidates who join the program.

industries.industry: Political consulting and campaign fundraising industries
industries.note: Candidates relying on voucher-funded small contributions would still need to spend them on campaign services, so the consulting industry keeps its market; candidates who stay outside the program would keep courting large donors as before.
